newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian farmers warn land row threatens exports.
newsitem.headline: Australian farmers warn land row threatens exports.

text.p: Australian farmers on Friday warned that attempts to paint their bitter struggle with Aborigines over native title land rights as a race issue threatened trade with Asian nations sensitive to "jingoism and xenophobia".

"The danger of the spread of misinformation is that it can be used by extreme elements in the community to create fear and loathing," National Farmers Federation president Donald McGauchie told foreign correspondents on Thursday.

"The rural sector, committed as it is to pursuing and capturing markets overseas, particularly those emerging markets in Asia...realises that the public canvassing of such extreme jingoism can have disastrous effects," McGauchie said.
"We must never forget that when we target Asia, we are targetting very sensitive communities, with disparate beliefs and customs," he said.

McGauchie warned that Asian nations, whose total food imports are expected to grow from their current A$10.3 billion (US$8.0 billion) to A$16.4 billion by the year 2000/2001, could easily favour suppliers without a history of racism.

"They hold all the cards in trade negotiations and they are not about to do any favours for a nation they perceive to support xenophobia whether it concerns economic policies or racial attitudes," he said.
Australia's rural exports account for a quarter of Australia's annual A$76 billion exports, but food exports only make up six percent of the burgeoning Asian food imports.

Australia's main rural exports to Asia are wool, wheat, sugar and meat and reach almost every major regional country, with Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China major importers. Live cattle exports are also a growing new trade to Indonesia and the Philippines.

Last December the High Court of Australia declared that Aboriginal native title existed on government land leased to farmers, contradicting the previously held belief that native title had been extinquished by pastoral leases.
McGauchie said farmers' objection to native title on their land was not based on race, but legal and economic issues, adding farmers rights to their land had been diminished.
"Farmers must have exclusive occupancy in order to manage their businesses...," McGauchie said.

"Like all urban businesses they need to know they have the ability to manage their businesses as they see fit and to diversify as circumstances change into areas such as agriforestry, farm tourism, station stores and contracting."
"We want what millions of people in our cities already have -- the legal ability to manage their business and plan for the future."

Up to 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square kms (2.96 million square miles) could be affected by native title claims. A total of 1,041 native title claims had been lodged since 1994, when the High Court first declared native title existed, but only one had been settled.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard has produced a 10-point native title plan in an attempt to find a compromise, but both Aborigines and farmers are still not satisfied.
The central elements of Howard's plan guarantee farmers rights to land leased from the government, while also giving Aborigines "native title" access for traditional uses.
Aborigines claim Howard's plan effectively extinguishes native title on pastoral land and farmers say it still leaves uncertainty over land ownership.
McGauchie said a major obstacle to finding a solution that will satisfy both sides was that land was an emotional issue for both farnmers and Aborigines.

"The native title goes to the deep feeling shared by both indigenous and non-indigenous people for their land and the essential role it plays...in the history of families throughout this country," McGauchie said.
